1.note: The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [give thanks to Yahweh for his covenant faithfulness is to forever]

The psalmist is using **to forever** as a common expression of his culture to mean “eternally” or “without end.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for his covenant faithfulness lasts forever]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way he is faithful to his covenant]

2.q: מִ֗י יְ֭מַלֵּל גְּבוּר֣וֹת יְהוָ֑ה יַ֝שְׁמִ֗יעַ כָּל־תְּהִלָּתֽ⁠וֹ
2.note: The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [No one can utter the mighty acts of Yahweh or proclaim all of his praise.]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [who can proclaim all of his praise]

Here, **praise** represents praiseworthy deeds. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [proclaim all of his praiseworthy deeds]

3.note: The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy or blessing. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy are] or [Truly blessed are]

The terms **guardians of justice** and **doers of righteousness** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are careful to do what is right]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [those who are always just]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [those who do what is right]

4.note: By **Remember me**, the psalmist is not implying that Yahweh forgot him, but he means for Yahweh to act favorably to him or to show him favor. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Pay attention to me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **favor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when you are kind to your people]

By **visit me**, the psalmist means “be kind to me” or “show favor to me.” You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [be kind to me]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when you save them]

5.note: The psalmist is using the adjective **good** as a noun to mean good things or good experiences. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to look on the good experiences] or [to look on the prosperity]

The psalmist is using the adjective **chosen** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [your chosen people]

The psalmist is using the adjective **gladness** as a noun to mean a certain kind of experience or state. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [when your nation becomes glad again]

Here the phrase **your inheritance** refers to the Israelites, the people who belong to Yahweh. When Yahweh saves them, they will **boast** about Yahweh. Alternate translation: [to boast of your greatness with your people] or [to boast with your people about you]

6.note: Here the psalmist is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [our ancestors]

The terms translated as **we have done wrong** and **we have done evil** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [we have continually done what is wrong]

The psalmist is using the adjectives **wrong** and **evil** as nouns to mean certain kinds of actions or behaviors. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [we have done what is wrong; we have done what is evil]

7.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **abundance** and **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in other ways. Alternate translation: [how you were constantly faithful to your covenant with them]

The terms **the sea** and **the Sea of Reeds** refer to the same place. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the Sea of Reeds]

8.note: Here, **his name** represents his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for the sake of his reputation]

Here, **to make known** marks **to make known his power** as the goal or purpose of **he saved them on account of his name**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order to make known]

The expression **to make known** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [so that everyone would know]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how powerful he is]

9.note: Here, **and it dried up** marks **it dried up** as the goal or purpose of **He rebuked the Sea of Reeds**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [He rebuked the Sea of Reeds so that it dried up]

The psalmist is making a comparison about how God led the Israelites through the dried-up sea. The point of this comparison is that just as **a desert** is dry land that can be walked on, so were **the depths** of the sea after God dried it up. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and it was as dry as a desert]

10.q: וַֽ֭⁠יּוֹשִׁיעֵ⁠ם מִ⁠יַּ֣ד שׂוֹנֵ֑א וַ֝⁠יִּגְאָלֵ֗⁠ם מִ⁠יַּ֥ד אוֹיֵֽב
10.note: These two phrases **he saved them from the hand of the hater** and **he rescued them from the hand of the enemy** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [So he saved them from the hand of the hater; yes, he rescued them from the hand of the enemy]

Here, **hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the power of … from the power of]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **hater**. He means haters in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [those who hated them]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **enemy**. He means enemies in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [their enemies]

11.note: The expression **one of them was not left** contains a passive verbal form. It means that none of them were left alive. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [all of them died]

12.note: Here, **words** represents what God said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what he had said to them]

Here, **praise** represents songs or words that praised God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [songs that praised him]

13.note: The phrases **they hurried, they forgot** express a single idea. The word **hurried** tells more about **forgot**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [But they quickly forgot]

14.note: These two phrases **in the wilderness** and **in the wasteland** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could indicate in some way that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [in the wilderness … in that wasteland]

The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [And they had strong cravings]

The implication is that they tested God’s patience and faithfulness by demanding things from him and complaining against him. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they pushed the limits of God’s patience with them]

15.note: The psalmist is speaking as if God literally **sent a wasting disease**. This means that God caused the disease to affect the Israelites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but he caused a wasting disease]

The psalmist is using **upon their lives** as a common expression of his culture to mean “that killed them” or “that took their lives.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that took their lives] or [that killed many of them]

16.note: The pronoun **they** refers to some of the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And some of the men became envious]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they also became envious of Aaron]

The psalmist is using the adjective **holy one** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the holy priest of Yahweh]

17.note: The psalmist is speaking as if the earth were a person who **swallowed** Dathan. He means that the earth opened up and Dathan fell into it and died. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and Dathan went down in it]
The words **Dathan** and **Abiram** are the names of men.

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **the congregation of Abiram** refers to Abiram’s followers who joined him in rebelling against Moses and Aaron. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the followers of Abiram]

18.note: These two phrases **Fire blazed up in their congregation** and **a flame burned up the wicked** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Fire blazed up in their congregation; indeed, a flame burned up the wicked]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those wicked people]

19.note: These two phrases **They made a calf at Horeb** and **worshiped a cast image** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [They made a calf at Horeb; yes, they worshiped that cast image]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that this **calf** was not a real calf but was made of gold as an idol to worship. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [They made a model of a calf]

The psalmist assumes that readers will know that **a cast image** refers to the golden calf that the Israelites made at Mount Horeb. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and worshiped that calf, which was a cast image]

20.note: The implication is that **their Glory** refers to God himself, who is glorious. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [their God, who is glorious,]

20.q: וַ⁠יָּמִ֥ירוּ אֶת־כְּבוֹדָ֑⁠ם בְּ⁠תַבְנִ֥ית שׁ֝֗וֹר אֹכֵ֥ל עֵֽשֶׂב
20.note: The psalmist is speaking of worshiping an idol rather than God as though they had **traded** God for this idol. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Thus they replaced worshiping their Glory with worshiping the likeness of a bull eating grass]

21.note: The psalmist is speaking as if the Israelites **forgot** God, that is, as if he had slipped from their memory. The psalmist means that they acted as if God did not exist or matter to them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They rejected God]

The implication is that God is the one who had done these great deeds to deliver the Israelites from Egypt. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [who had done great deeds]

22.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **wonders**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [wonderful things]

The implication is that the land of Ham refers to Egypt, since Ham was the ancestor of the Egyptians according to biblical genealogies. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in the land where Ham’s descendants lived]

23.note: The implication is that God was determined to destroy the Israelites because of their sin, but Moses interceded for them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [So he intended to annihilate them] or [So he would have annihilated them]

The psalmist says **had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach** to introduce a situation that did not happen in order to help explain what would have happened if Moses had not interceded for the Israelites. Use a natural method in your language for introducing a situation that did not happen. Alternate translation: [if Moses, his chosen one, had not stood in the breach]

The expression **his chosen one** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [the one whom God had chosen]

The psalmist is using **stood in the breach** as a common expression of his culture to mean “defended them” or “interceded for them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [defended them]
Here, **to his face** represents being in God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before God]

The psalmist is using **to turn away his heat** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to turn away his anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to keep him from destroying them in his anger]

24.note: Here, **word** represents what God said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what he had said]

25.note: By **they did not listen to the voice**, the psalmist means they did not obey or heed what Yahweh said. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [they did not heed the voice of]

Here, **the voice of Yahweh** represents what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to what Yahweh said to them]

26.note: The phrase **raised his hand** describes a symbolic action by which God showed that he was making a solemn oath or vow to the Israelites. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Then he made an oath to them]

The psalmist is using **to make them fall** as a common expression of his culture to mean “to kill them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to kill them]

27.note: These two phrases **to make their seed fall among the nations** and **to scatter them among the lands** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [and to scatter their descendants among people of foreign lands]

The psalmist is speaking of the descendants of the Israelites as if they were **seed** that would fall and be scattered as a farmer scatters seed on a field. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to spread their descendants]

Here, **the nations** represents the people of foreign nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [among people of foreign nations]

28.note: The psalmist is speaking as if the Israelites had **joined themselves** to the Baal of Peor, that is, as if they were attaching themselves physically to the idol. The psalmist means that they gave their loyalty and devotion to this false god. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They gave their loyalty]

This could mean: (1) the people worshiped their dead ancestors and treated them as gods. Alternate translation: [the sacrifices given to dead ancestors] or (2) the psalmist is describing Baal and the people’s other idols as dead. Alternate translation: [sacrifices given to lifeless idols]

The psalmist is using the adjective **dead** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the sacrifices for dead people]

The psalmist is using this possessive form to mean sacrifices offered to idols, which were considered to be dead gods. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the sacrifices given to those who had died]

29.note: Some ancient manuscripts read **And they angered**. The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “And they angered him.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [And they angered him]

The psalmist is using **a plague broke out among them** as a common expression of his culture to mean “many of them became sick with a plague.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and many of them became sick with a plague]

The implication is that God sent the plague as judgment for their sinful actions. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and Yahweh afflicted them with a plague]

30.note: The psalmist is speaking of Phinehas as if he had **stood** up from a sitting position. The psalmist means that Phinehas took action courageously to intervene in the situation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Then Phinehas showed his courage]

The implication is that Phinehas acted on behalf of Yahweh to stop the plague by executing judgment on those who were sinning. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and acted on behalf of Yahweh]

The expression **the plague was restrained** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [and the plague stopped]

31.note: The expression **It was counted to him** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People credited it to him]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [as a righteous deed]

The psalmist is using **to generation and generation** as a common expression of his culture to mean “throughout all generations” or “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and will be so throughout all generations]

32.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And they angered Yahweh]
The word **Meribah** is the name of a place. Alternate translation: [the place called Meribah]
The pronoun **it** refers to what happened at the waters of Meribah. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and what happened there was bad for Moses]

33.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation of what happened to Moses at the waters of Meribah. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [What happened was that]
Here, **his** could refer to: (1) Moses. Alternate translation: [they rebelled against Moses’ spirit] or (2) Yahweh. Alternate translation: [they rebelled against Yahweh’s Spirit]

Some ancient manuscripts read **they rebelled against his spirit**. The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “they embittered his spirit.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [they embittered his spirit]

Here, **his spirit** represents him as a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they rebelled against him]

It might seem that the expression **with his lips** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and he spoke rashly]
Here the pronouns **he** and **his** refer to Moses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and Moses spoke rashly with his lips]

35.note: The psalmist is speaking as if the Israelites had **mingled** or mixed themselves physically with the nations. He means that they intermarried with people from other nations and adopted their religious and cultural practices. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but they intermarried with people of the nations]

Here, **the nations** represents the people of those nations. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [but they intermarried with the people of the other nations]

36.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the idols, while the pronoun **them** refers to the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the idols became a snare to the people]

The psalmist is speaking of the idols as if they were **a snare** that could trap the Israelites and destroy them. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this in plain language. Alternate translation: [and that was the beginning of their destruction]

37.note: The pronoun **they** refers to the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Our ancestors sacrificed]

38.note: Here, **blood** represents the lives of people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They killed innocent people]

Here, **idols** represents the spiritual beings that the people believed the idols represented. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [whom they sacrificed to the spirits that the people of Canaan worshiped]

By **the land was desecrated by bloodshed**, the psalmist means that the land became unfit for God’s people to live in because of the murders committed there. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and the land became unfit for the people of God to live in because they murdered people there]

39.note: These two phrases **And they became unclean by their deeds** and **and they prostituted themselves by their actions** mean basically the same thing. The second phrase emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [And they became unclean by their deeds; indeed, they prostituted themselves by their actions]

The psalmist is speaking as if the Israelites had **become unclean** physically through their sinful actions. He means that they became spiritually defiled or morally corrupted by their idolatrous practices. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they became very sinful]

The psalmist is speaking as if the Israelites were unfaithful wives who **prostituted themselves**. He means that they violated their covenant relationship with Yahweh by worshiping idols. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they violated their relationship with Yahweh]

40.note: The psalmist is using the phrase **Yahweh’s nose burned** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Yahweh was angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [So Yahweh was very angry]

The psalmist is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were Yahweh’s **inheritance**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people who belonged to him]

41.note: Here, **hand** represents the power and control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he gave them into the control of people of other nations]

The psalmist is using the verb **haters** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use verbs in the same way. If not, you can translate this with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and people who hated them]

42.note: These two phrases **And their enemies oppressed them** and **and they were humbled under their hand** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [And their enemies oppressed them; yes, they were humbled under their hand]

The expression **they were humbled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the hand of their enemies humbled them]

Here, **hand** represents the power and control of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they were humbled under their control]

43.note: The psalmist is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the verb translated as **they were rebellious** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the contrast between God’s repeated rescue and the people’s persistent rebellion. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [but those people, they were rebellious]

The implication is that the Israelites were rebellious in their plans and decisions against God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in their thinking]

The psalmist is speaking as if the Israelites were objects that **sank** down into something. He means that they became more and more deeply involved in sinful behavior. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and their sinfulness became progressively worse]

44.note: The psalmist is using **in the narrow to them** as a common expression of his culture to mean “when they were in distress” or “when they were in trouble.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that these things were very hard for them]

The implication is that the Israelites were crying out to God for help during their distress. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [when he was hearing them cry out to him in distress]

45.note: By **he remembered**, the psalmist means that God was mindful of his covenant, that he acted because of his covenant, not that he had forgotten about it and then remembered. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And he called to mind]

By **relented**, the psalmist means that God turned away from his anger and chose not to continue punishing his people. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and held back from punishing them further]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **abundance** and **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [because he is so abundantly faithful to his covenant]

46.note: The psalmist is using **gave them for compassion** as a common expression of his culture to mean “caused them to be treated with compassion” or “made them objects of compassion.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He made them objects of compassion]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He made all of their captors compassionate toward them]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in the thinking or consideration of their captors. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the thinking of all of their captors]

47.note: Here, **to give thanks** marks giving thanks to God’s holy name as the goal or purpose of **Gather us from the nations**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order that we may give thanks]

The psalmist is using the possessive form to describe a **name** that is characterized by **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to give thanks to your holy name]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who God is or to refer to God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to give thanks to you, the one who is known to be holy]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praises**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to be proud about praising you]

48.note: The expression **be blessed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May people bless Yahweh, the God of Israel]

The psalmist is not using this possessive form **the God of Israel** to indicate that the Israelites possess or control God. Rather the psalmist is using these words to indicate that God is the one whom Israel worships. Alternate translation: [who is the God whom Israel worships]

The psalmist is using **from everlasting and to everlasting** as a common expression of his culture to mean “for all eternity.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for all eternity]

The words **Amen. Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Amen. Halleluia] or [May it be so. Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]
